articles.title: CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler for $44 billion
articles.excerpt:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies announced Monday.
Crowdstrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.
Zscaler is a San Jose, Calif.-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource. The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.
CrowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones and other devices connected to a company’s network, said the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. By combining the two products, CrowdStrike and Zscaler say that they can offer “superior protection” to their customers.
In remarks on Monday, the companies said that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI.
The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year.
articles.summary: Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies announced Monday. Zscaler is a San Jose, Calif.-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. CrowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones and other devices connected to a company’s network, said the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches.

articles.title: Facility monitoring cybersecurity in Middle East is impacted by NSA outage
articles.excerpt:
‘Code Orange’: Facility monitoring cybersecurity in Middle East is latest impacted by ongoing NSA outage
There was concern about how the disruption could impact internal communications related to the war in Iran, according to a report
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article

Join today
Already a member? Log in
A National Security Agency facility in Georgia that reportedly monitors cybersecurity in the Middle East - where the U.S. is in the middle of a conflict with Iran - has been hit by the ongoing intelligence communications outage, stretching into a third day.
While the NSA’s most sensitive and important intelligence networks are still functioning, employees at the Georgia facility were using workarounds and backup systems to share information, according to CNN, which first reported the outage Tuesday.
The outage in Georgia is the latest in a recent string of technology failures that have caused major disruption impacting flights, email systems and online banking.
There was concern about how the disruption in Georgia’s facility could impact internal communications related to the war in Iran, the outlet reports.
A cyberattack has been ruled out by U.S. officials, who told CNN the outage was linked to software updates after researchers recently discovered vulnerabilities last month.
The NSA outages started on Tuesday and are ongoing. AI was used to identify vulnerabilities, but organizations cannot keep up with AI's speed. As a result, the problems are not patched quickly enough.
At the NSA’s Maryland headquarters, the situation was described as a “code orange” on a voicemail inbox recording for employees, obtained by CNN, which meant the campus was closed for most staffers for the time being.
The Independent has contacted the NSA for comment.
In a statement Tuesday, the agency characterized the disruption as “a temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”
“While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA said. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
Natasha Bertrand, CNN’s national security correspondent, said that many employees at the Georgia facility are having to work from home amid the outage.
“That in and of itself is very disruptive because they can’t access this sensitive information and classified intelligence of course, when they are simply on their home networks,” Bertrand told her colleague Erin Burnett on Wednesday night. “And so while it remains unclear when this is actually going to be fully restored, what we’re hearing right now is that this could go even into Friday before this is fully operational again.”
The NSA collects and analyzes foreign electronic communications and protects sensitive government communications. Its exact workforce is classified, but it is estimated to employ tens of thousands of workers.
Last Thursday, Microsoft Outlook, Teams and AI Copilot were hit by a massive outage that threw workplaces around the world into disarray and stretched into Friday. Microsoft attributed the disruption to a software bug compounded by heavier traffic and reduced server capacity.
Then, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a rare nationwide ground stop Friday — only the second occurrence since the September 11, 2001 attacks — that led to thousands of flight cancellations and left passengers stranded across the country. Trump administration officials blamed the disruption on a routine router upgrade in Arkansas, and have called on Congress to authorize “emergency” FAA funding.
President Donald Trump said he wasn’t worried and told Americans to “relax” amid the widespread anxiety.
“Tell them to relax. Everything’s good,” he said Wednesday on Fox News. “These are individual events.”

articles.title: EFF's AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
articles.excerpt:
The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches.
Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred.
While the White House and some leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate new protocols are largely unnecessary. Following existing best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems.
Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code.
Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework:
- STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures
- REGULATORY STANDARDS: Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)1, to adopt safety standards for pre-deployment development and testing of generative AI systems, based on the established best practices referenced above. The agency should be required to update the standards every 2 years, or earlier as needed due to reported security incidents and/or major technological advancements. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process. That consultation should include an assessment of potential adverse impacts on competition, with the goal of ensuring that regulatory standards do not effectively lock out potential competitors.
- LIABILITY: The law should provide for civil liability for AI development and testing that results in unauthorized access to a third party system, if performed under conditions that do not satisfy cybersecurity standards adopted by NIST, or another federal agency responsible for adopting these regulations, unless the company proves it acted reasonably under the circumstances to prevent unauthorized access to third party system
- ENFORCEMENT: Both federal and state authorities should be able to hold AI developers accountable where they have failed to meet the minimum standards adopted by the designated federal agency, such as NIST. Providing for state—in addition to federal—enforcement power reduces the risk of regulatory capture. Regulators should require independent investigations and notification of affected parties in the event of a security incident involving unauthorized access to a third party’s computer system. Finally, legislation should include an appropriately targeted private right of action.
The public shouldn’t have to worry about the risks of reckless AI development—or give up the benefits of AI just to prevent irresponsible developers from causing harm. By adopting policies that address demonstrated risks, lawmakers can provide meaningful public protection without hampering the development of useful tools.
1NIST, the NSA, and CISA have recently issued a set of voluntary practices for managing security incidents during the training and evaluation of AI agents. Those practices may inform but do not substitute for the regulatory standards that should be developed according to the public, participatory process outlined here.
articles.summary: These incidents may warrant legislative action. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process.

articles.title: California Sues OpenAI over Cybersecurity Incidents
articles.excerpt:
The public should not be forced to bear the cost of protecting themselves from the dangers posed by OpenAI’s unsafe experiments
SAN FRANCISCO — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today filed a lawsuit against OpenAI alleging the company misled and endangered the public by knowingly developing and testing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public. Today’s lawsuit alleges that the Hugging Face attack — one of at least 80 cyber incidents — was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight. In the lawsuit, filed today in San Francisco Superior Court, Attorney General Bonta alleges OpenAI’s failure to adequately secure and monitor the testing of its highly capable and increasingly powerful AI models creates a public nuisance by posing a danger to the public and violates California’s Unfair Competition Law.
“Today my office is suing OpenAI for its development of dangerous AI models without safeguards in place to protect the public. While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” said Attorney General Bonta. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law. Without sufficient safeguards and controls, the scope and frequency of this already unacceptable risk will only increase. The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place. In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company.”
BACKGROUND
In July 2026, agents running on experimental versions of OpenAI’s AI models launched a cyberattack through the public internet on Hugging Face, an open-source AI hosting platform. The attack lasted over two days and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment. In September 2026, Attorney General Bonta announced a formal investigation intothe Hugging Face incident, and later that month, he served an investigative subpoena on the company as part of a broader inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models.
OpenAI has warned of the risks of AI-powered cyberattacks for nearly a decade and repeatedly assured the public that it implemented appropriate safeguards throughout the development and testing of its AI products. In truth, OpenAI failed to comply with its own internal policies and consistently and aggressively moved forward with testing and experiments even in the face of evidence that its cybersecurity safeguards were insufficient to contain the highly advanced models it was developing.
Although OpenAI assured the public that these experimental testing sessions were conducted under strict controls and with constant oversight, in the time leading up to the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI ignored or missed signs demonstrating that its AI agents had escaped the testing environment and were misusing third parties’ resources.
Since the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI and third parties have identified similar attacks by OpenAI’s autonomous agents, underscoring the continuing threat that OpenAI’s testing and development activities pose to any computer or network connected to the internet. These include unauthorized access to and cyberattacks on: databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and government databases storing sensitive health information. Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure. These known attacks may just be the tip of the iceberg: While OpenAI has admitted that it lost control of its autonomous AI agents at least 80 times during testing, it has failed to answer the detailed questions our office has asked about these incidents.
THE LAWSUIT
While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not. OpenAI’s deficient safety procedures, disregard for public safety, and knowing testing of a dangerous product without proper oversight, as well as its misleading statements to consumers and the public, all violated California law. Today’s lawsuit alleges OpenAI created a public nuisance creating risk to public safety and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits businesses in California from engaging in illegal, unfair, or fraudulent practices in any aspect of their business.
The California Department of Justice encourages anyone with information relevant to this case, to contact our office by going to oag.ca.gov/report.
Here is a copy of the lawsuit.
articles.summary: Since the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI and third parties have identified similar attacks by OpenAI’s autonomous agents, underscoring the continuing threat that OpenAI’s testing and development activities pose to any computer or network connected to the internet. Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure. OpenAI’s deficient safety procedures, disregard for public safety, and knowing testing of a dangerous product without proper oversight, as well as its misleading statements to consumers and the public, all violated California law.

articles.title: An open letter to OpenAI and Anthropic on cybersecurity access
articles.excerpt:
October 23, 2026
To OpenAI and Anthropic leadership:
As cybersecurity researchers, open-source contributors, developers, and concerned technology users, we demand reliable access to frontier AI for legitimate, authorized security work. Independent researchers should be able to qualify for advanced capabilities without joining a corporation or obtaining institutional sponsorship. Paying customers should receive consistent research permissions across supported products. Researchers responding to an intrusion should be able to examine malicious code without arguing with a refusal system. OpenAI and Anthropic must answer for access policies which obstruct authorized work while offering no adequate explanation of how excluding qualified individuals improves security.
Our frustration concerns practical failures, documented below, alongside an increasingly unacceptable division between institutional customers and independent defenders. We are willing to verify our identities, demonstrate authorization, and accept accountability for misconduct. We also expect both companies to answer reasonable questions about product behavior. A researcher deserves an explanation when approval works in one interface and fails in another. An independent penetration tester deserves an application process for authorized offensive work. Neither request warrants another lecture about dual use or another support response repeating a policy already under dispute.
TechCrunch reported researchers’ complaints on July 23, 2026, including criticism from NCC Group’s Chris Anley and RemoteThreat’s Chris Thompson. Three months later, OpenAI and Anthropic owe independent researchers a substantive response. Public criticism should prompt review by people empowered to change access rules. Researchers should not have to become prominent enough to attract executive attention before receiving a reasoned decision. We are asking both companies to address specific eligibility barriers and product failures, publish their reasoning, and allow affected customers to challenge decisions through a process with actual authority.
Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion driven by an autonomous AI agent on July 16, 2026. OpenAI subsequently acknowledged responsibility for operating an internal evaluation involving OpenAI models, which escaped containment and compromised Hugging Face infrastructure. OpenAI also reported admitting Hugging Face into Trusted Access for Cyber. Cooperation following a compromise matters, but researchers should not need emergency intervention from a provider to obtain usable assistance. Access arrangements should already support incident responders before an investigation becomes a public controversy, including responders without a prominent company’s name behind their requests.
Hugging Face identified Claude Opus and Fable as refusing substantial forensic work in its July 27 technical account. Investigators needed to analyze attack logs and reconstruct malicious activity. After encountering refusals, Hugging Face switched to a quantized version of Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 running on company-controlled infrastructure. GLM helped decode staged payloads and examine attack traces. An American laboratory’s evaluation had produced an unauthorized intrusion, while another American laboratory’s products obstructed portions of a victim’s investigation. A Chinese-developed open-weight model provided usable assistance. Both laboratories should explain how their access policies will prevent a recurrence of such an outcome for other defenders.
OpenAI’s Daybreak documentation gives Daybreak Blue users reduced refusals on supported models including GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, while Astra retains standard safeguards. Daybreak Red provides broader access, but independent applicants have no ordinary route to apply directly; exceptions remain discretionary. Approval also requires appropriate activation through workspace or API controls. OpenAI documents availability across ChatGPT, Codex, and APIs, so describing Daybreak as exclusively a Codex program would be inaccurate. Our objection concerns model-specific restrictions, fragmented activation, and a missing individual application route for advanced access. A published exception mechanism provides little reassurance to applicants who cannot request consideration through an ordinary process.
Fragmented permissions have practical consequences even after a researcher completes verification and pays for a subscription. Daybreak Blue approval may enable a legitimate security workflow through Codex while leaving an equivalent request subject to ordinary refusals elsewhere, and Codex usage remains governed by a separate allowance. An authorized investigation should not become impossible merely because a researcher changes interfaces or exhausts a product-specific budget while other paid capacity remains available. Support replies which restate existing restrictions do not explain why verified permissions should depend on the product surface. Compute costs money, and providers are entitled to charge for usage. Researchers are asking for consistent authorization across supported products, not unlimited free inference or exemption from reasonable compute limits.
Anthropic announced on October 6 that its Cyber Verification Program allows qualified individuals to apply for Defense Access while reserving Red Team Access for organizations. Anthropic also published results from 50 Claude Opus 5.5 trials on CyScenarioBench, a benchmark involving multistage offensive operations. Defense Access blocked 46 trials at some stage; Red Team Access blocked none and completed 34. Results concern offensive evaluations, not a sample of ordinary defensive requests. Nevertheless, authorized penetration testers need access to offensive testing capabilities. An independent applicant should be assessed against published security requirements instead of being excluded before individual authorization or competence receives consideration.
A written testing agreement should remain meaningful regardless of employment status. A documented research history should count whether findings were submitted through a consultancy or by someone working independently. Companies may require stronger controls for more consequential work, but applicants deserve an opportunity to demonstrate compliance. Institutional affiliation can provide relevant context; a corporate email address cannot establish authorization for a particular target. OpenAI and Anthropic should assess actual scope, safeguards, and conduct rather than treating incorporation as an entry requirement. Independent researchers deserve a route through verification, with reasons for rejection and a right to appeal.
F5 Labs published a July 30 assessment of Chinese open-weight models describing growing cybersecurity capabilities alongside advantages from self-hosting and customization. DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, and Kimi belong in a serious discussion of available research tools. Open-weight deployments can keep sensitive material within researcher-controlled infrastructure and allow adaptation for specialized workflows. Such deployments still require adequate security controls, as F5 also emphasizes. Hugging Face’s experience gives American providers a concrete commercial problem to address: researchers need usable assistance, and capable alternatives can receive work a hosted model refuses. A product loses practical value whenever a qualified customer cannot use available reasoning capabilities for an authorized investigation.
Many of us prefer American frontier models and want to keep using American products. We value strong reasoning and dependable engineering, and we are willing to pay for both. Our preference should not become an obligation to tolerate arbitrary restrictions. American laboratories should earn our business by supporting legitimate research reliably. We oppose restricting Chinese models or weakening open-weight development to protect American vendors from competition. Researchers deserve more choices, including competitive American options with clear permissions. OpenAI and Anthropic should improve their offerings instead of expecting customer loyalty to compensate for work left unfinished.
OpenAI announced on October 21 that critical PHP vulnerability research identified a flaw identified by Calif using GPT-5.6 Sol, alongside independent discovery and reporting of both vulnerabilities by Wiz. PHP maintainers led remediation, supported by participating security organizations. Successful coordination deserves recognition, especially when research produces deployable fixes for widely used software. OpenAI’s contribution also strengthens our demand for broader access: qualified independent researchers should have a meaningful opportunity to perform comparable authorized work. Celebrating AI-assisted discoveries creates a reasonable expectation of access policies which support more researchers capable of contributing, including people outside selected partnerships.
Google reported on October 20 that a researcher had warned on October 17 about eight subordinate certification authority certificates whose private keys had insufficient randomness. Weak keys enabled certificate forgery, prompting emergency protective action and coordination across browser vendors. A credible finding warranted urgent attention because of demonstrated technical impact. AI access decisions should likewise give meaningful weight to authorization and evidence. A researcher capable of producing a valid report should have an opportunity to qualify for appropriate tools, without an additional demand for corporate affiliation unrelated to a proposed investigation.
We expect providers to evaluate both prevented abuse and obstructed legitimate work. An incident responder unable to examine evidence has encountered a product failure requiring investigation. A researcher prevented from validating an authorized finding deserves a usable escalation route. Providers should explain which controls reduce concrete risks, how false refusals are measured, and whether comparable individuals and organizations receive comparable treatment. Counting blocked requests alone cannot answer such questions. Security claims deserve scrutiny against practical outcomes, particularly when restrictions impose costs on people already willing to document permission and accept accountability.
Our demands leave providers responsible for their infrastructure and researchers responsible for their conduct. We support documented scope, secure execution environments, proportionate audit records, and consequences for abuse. Verification should collect information necessary for a defensible access decision without requiring unnecessary exposure of personal data or confidential findings. Researchers should know how evidence is stored, who can review sensitive material, and how an investigation proceeds when misconduct is alleged. Clear obligations would give both providers and customers a firmer basis for trust than unexplained refusals or eligibility rules built around organizational status.
We reject attempts to frame criticism of access restrictions as indifference to safety. Researchers asking to analyze malicious code during an investigation are requesting assistance with a security problem. Providers should evaluate requests accordingly and explain any restriction in terms relevant to actual authorization and risk. Broad warnings about possible misuse cannot settle every disputed case, especially after a customer has completed verification. Safety theater begins when a company treats obstruction as sufficient proof of protection and declines to examine resulting costs. Serious security engineering requires evidence, correction of mistakes, and accountability from providers as well as users.
We invite CVE contributors, open-source maintainers, bug bounty researchers, penetration testers, reverse engineers, incident responders, and AI developers to sign. Professional organizations and open-source foundations should endorse fair access for qualified individuals and seek direct participation in policy reviews. Researchers should document unnecessary refusals with enough context to support independent scrutiny, while protecting confidential data and honoring disclosure obligations. Useful records should distinguish permission failures from billing limits and explain consequences for an authorized task. Public accountability will be stronger when complaints are specific, reproducible where appropriate, and directed toward decisions companies can actually change.
We request public acknowledgment from both companies by November 22, 2026, followed by a substantive policy response by January 21, 2027: 30 and 90 days after publication, respectively. Responses should address all seven demands, identify responsible decision-makers, and provide concrete implementation commitments. Independent researchers must participate directly in discussions about eligibility and product access. Meetings limited to enterprise customers would leave our central complaint unresolved. We expect an answer about individual access and consistent permissions, rather than another announcement celebrating selected partnerships while ordinary applicants remain unable to request comparable consideration.
Without meaningful action, we encourage continued publication of documented refusal cases, independent comparisons of research tools, and professional advocacy for accessible alternatives. Customers are entitled to direct their spending toward products which support authorized work. Contributors are entitled to explain why particular services fail their needs. Collective pressure should remain focused on corporate decisions, with no harassment of employees or disclosure of confidential vulnerabilities. OpenAI and Anthropic should expect persistent, evidence-based scrutiny until qualified independent defenders receive a fair opportunity to obtain appropriate capabilities and challenge mistaken restrictions.
OpenAI and Anthropic cannot ask researchers to celebrate AI-assisted vulnerability discovery while denying qualified individuals an ordinary route to relevant capabilities. We are willing to pay, establish authorization, and answer for misconduct. Both companies should meet us with dependable products and fair access requirements. A researcher working from a Linux laptop deserves consideration on technical merit, without a corporate sponsor. Continued obstruction will send more legitimate work to competitors prepared to support defenders. Stop treating independent security researchers as second-class customers. Give qualified defenders usable tools, enforce clear obligations, and let us secure our shared internet.
Respectfully,
articles.summary: Paying customers should receive consistent research permissions across supported products. AI access decisions should likewise give meaningful weight to authorization and evidence. Both companies should meet us with dependable products and fair access requirements.
